title: Strict local curve reduction and costalk identifications
statement:
Let $\ell$ be a prime, $\Lambda=\mathbf F_\ell$, and $X$ a Noetherian excellent scheme on which $\ell$ is invertible [def-exc-excellent-ring]. Noetherian means having a finite affine cover by spectra of Noetherian rings [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], and excellent means having an affine cover by spectra of excellent rings. On small etale derived categories [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories], for a closed immersion $a:W\hookrightarrow V$ with complementary open $b$, write $a^!$ for the right derived functor of $a^{-1}\ker(1\to b_*b^{-1})$ on $\Lambda$-module sheaves [def-pur-etale-supported-kernel], [def-weil-closed-immersion]. For a point $z$ and $K\in D^+(X_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)$, put $C_z(K)=i_z^!(K|_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{X,z}})$, where $i_z:\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(z)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{X,z}$ is the closed point [def-weil-residue-field]. For a geometric point $\bar z$ above $z$, let $C_{\bar z}(K)$ be its geometric fibre [def-weil-geometric-point]. There is a natural isomorphism
$$C_{\bar z}(K)\simeq R\Gamma_{\{z_0\}}(X_{(\bar z)},K|_{X_{(\bar z)}}),$$
where $X_{(\bar z)}$ is the strict localization [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit], $z_0$ its closed point, and supported cohomology is [def-pur-etale-derived-supported-sections].

Suppose $\bar y\rightsquigarrow\bar x$ is a geometric specialization, meaning an $X$-map $X_{(\bar y)}\to X_{(\bar x)}$, and is immediate, meaning that the reduced closure $Z$ of the image of $\bar y$ in $X_{(\bar x)}$ has Krull dimension $1$ (the supremum of lengths of chains of irreducible closed subsets). Let $i:Z\hookrightarrow X_{(\bar x)}$ and $L=i^!(K|_{X_{(\bar x)}})$. Then $Z$ is an integral excellent strictly henselian local scheme of dimension $1$ [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology]. Its normalization $\nu:\widetilde Z\to Z$ in its function field [def-sc-normalization] is finite and a universal homeomorphism [def-weil-universal-homeomorphism]; $\widetilde Z$ is the spectrum of a strictly henselian discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring]. The generic point is unchanged. If $z_0$ and $\widetilde z_0$ are the closed points, then $\kappa(\widetilde z_0)/\kappa(z_0)$ is finite purely inseparable, of degree a power of the residue characteristic (degree $1$ in characteristic zero), hence its degree is invertible in $\Lambda$.

Inverse image along $\nu$ is an equivalence of etale sheaf categories. With the geometric points induced by the specialization and its unique lift to $\widetilde Z$, there are natural isomorphisms
$$C_{\bar y}(K)\simeq C_{\bar y}(L)\simeq(\nu^*L)_{\bar\eta},\qquad C_{\bar x}(K)\simeq C_{\bar x}(L)\simeq R\Gamma_{\{\widetilde z_0\}}(\widetilde Z,\nu^*L).$$
On the middle terms $C$ is computed on $Z$. These isomorphisms respect the Tate twists defined by roots of unity [def-asd-finite-etale-tate-twist] (negative twists mean dual tensor powers) and the cohomological shifts.

source.place: Expose XVII, Definition 1.1.1 and its footnote, section 1.3 before Definition 1.3.1, and Definition 1.4.1 with its costalk comparison square (printed pp. 258–262; n=ell)

proof.text:
First fix the support calculus used below. The adjunction and supported-sheaf identification in [lem-pur-etale-supported-kernel-adjunction] hold also for $A$-module sheaves: its natural bijection on underlying abelian-group morphisms restricts to the $A$-linear morphisms, since it intertwines multiplication by each scalar. Closed pushforward is exact on modules because it is exact on underlying abelian sheaves. Thus [lem-sp-right-adjoint-preserves-injectives] shows that the support right adjoint takes module injectives to injectives. On an injective resolution $I$, one has degreewise $\Gamma(W,a^!_0I)=\ker(I(V)\to I(V\setminus W))$. Hence
$$R\Gamma(W,a^!K)\cong R\Gamma_W(V,K).$$
For composable closed immersions $a,b$, [lem-cat-right-adjoint-composition] gives $(ab)^!\cong b^!a^!$: the corresponding underived identity derives on these same injective resolutions. The isomorphism preserves the pasted counits. This uses no purity or constructibility.

source.place: Definition 1.1.1; support adjunction expanded using Stacks Tags 09XP and 09XQ

proof.text:
For any point $z$, write $V=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{X,z}$ and $q:T=X_{(\bar z)}\to V$. Choosing an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}D$ at $z$, [lem-exc-affine-strict-local-ring-comparison] identifies $T$ over $V$ with the spectrum of the algebraic strict henselization of $\mathcal O_{X,z}=D_{\mathfrak p}$ relative to the separable closure of $\kappa(z)$ in the geometric point. The pointed-neighbourhood construction [lem-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-triples], taken with $R=\mathcal O_{X,z}$ and its maximal ideal, makes $q$ ind-etale and gives $\mathfrak m_T=\mathfrak m_V\mathcal O_T$, so the base change of the closed point of $V$ is the spectrum $s_0$ of that separable residue closure. The schemes $V,T$ are Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-noetherian] and [lem-sc-strict-henselization-noetherian]. Apply [lem-per-ind-etale-closed-support-base-change] to the closed point immersion of $V$. Pulling its result to the chosen geometric point identifies $C_{\bar z}(K)$ with the geometric fibre of $s_0^!(K|_T)$. Since $s_0$ has separably closed residue field, [lem-weil-pbc-strictly-henselian-sections-stalk] identifies that fibre with its sections; that sections functor is exact because it is a stalk. Apply Step 1 to get
$$C_{\bar z}(K)\cong R\Gamma_{\{z_0\}}(T,K|_T).$$
The sections/stalk comparison is $A$-linear by naturality in scalar multiplication.

source.place: Definition 1.1.1 and footnote; geometric fibre equals strict-local cohomology with closed support

proof.text: Now put $T=X_{(\bar x)}=\operatorname{Spec}H$. Choose an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}R$ of $X$ at $x$. The chart can be chosen excellent by the definition of excellence and localization, [lem-exc-finite-type-localization-excellent]. The strict-henselization chart is ind-etale by [lem-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-affine-chart-ind-etale], hence weakly etale by [lem-weil-pbc-ind-etale-stability]. Its ring $H$ is Noetherian by Step 2. Thus [lem-exc-weakly-etale-excellent] makes $H$ excellent. Let $\mathfrak p\subset H$ be the image of $\bar y$. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-irreducible-closed-subsets-primes], the reduced closure is $Z=\operatorname{Spec}(H/\mathfrak p)$. This is an integral local scheme of dimension one by the immediate-specialization hypothesis. It is excellent by [lem-exc-finite-type-localization-excellent], and strictly henselian by [lem-weil-pbc-quotient-henselian-pair]: the quotient has the same separably closed residue field as $H$.

source.place: Definition 1.4.1: the reduced one-dimensional closure inside the strict localization

proof.text: Write $B=H/\mathfrak p$, $F=\operatorname{Frac}B$, and $N$ for the integral closure of $B$ in $F$; thus $\widetilde Z=\operatorname{Spec}N$ by [def-sc-normalization]. Excellence implies Nagata by [lem-exc-quasi-excellent-nagata]. The Nagata domain $B$ is N-2 by [lem-weil-pbc-nagata-domain-n2]; taking the degree-one extension $F/F$ in [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain] makes $N$ a finite $B$-module. Hence $\nu$ is finite. Apply [lem-sc-integral-closure-dedekind-surjective-fibres] with $L=F$: $N$ is a Noetherian normal domain of dimension one, its fraction field is $F$, and its spectrum is surjective over $\operatorname{Spec}B$ with finite residue extensions. Since a domain has no idempotents except $0,1$, [lem-trf-integral-component-henselian-permanence] makes $N$ strictly henselian local. Finally [lem-sc-normal-dim1-dvr] makes $N$ a DVR. Thus normalization really gives a strictly henselian trait, not a product of traits.

source.place: Section 1.3 before Definition 1.3.1: finite normalization is a strictly henselian trait

proof.text: Both $B$ and $N$ are local domains of dimension one. Their spectra have just the zero prime and the maximal ideal: any other nonzero prime would give a chain of length two. The zero prime of $N$ contracts to zero and has residue field $F$; the maximal ideal contracts to that of $B$ by the local-map conclusion in Step 4. Thus $\nu$ is bijective on points and is the identity at the generic point. Its closed residue extension is finite by Step 4 and purely inseparable by [lem-kun-sep-closed-finite-extension-purely-inseparable], since the residue field of $B$ is separably closed. Consequently $\nu$ is radicial by [def-weil-radicial-morphism]. It is integral and surjective by Step 4, so [lem-pc-integral-radicial-surjective-universal-homeomorphism] makes it a universal homeomorphism. The unique lift of any given geometric closed point follows from [lem-weil-pbc-sepclosed-finite-extension-unique-embedding].

source.place: Section 1.3: universal homeomorphism and purely inseparable closed residue extension

proof.text: Let $d=[\kappa(\widetilde z_0):\kappa(z_0)]$. In characteristic zero the purely inseparable extension is trivial by the definition [def-pc-field-tower], so $d=1$. In positive characteristic $p$, [lem-weil-pbc-purely-inseparable-pth-root-tower] expresses the extension as a finite tower of degree-$p$ extensions. Multiplication of degrees [lem-weil-pbc-field-degree-multiplicativity] gives $d=p^r$ where $r$ is the length of that tower (including $r=0$). Since $\ell$ is a unit on $Z$, $p\ne\ell$, and the residue class of $p^r$ in $\mathbf F_\ell$ is nonzero and hence invertible. This proves the claimed invertibility without assuming the residue fields perfect.

source.place: Section 1.3 and Definition 1.3.1: the degree used to normalize the transition is invertible

proof.text: For $w=x$ or $y$, let $t$ be its induced point on $T$ and its point on $Z$. The structural map $T\to X$ is locally ind-etale by Step 3, so [lem-trf-ind-etale-strict-local-invariance] identifies $T_{(\bar t)}$ with $X_{(\bar w)}$, including their closed geometric points. Step 2 therefore identifies the costalk of $K$ on $X$ with that of $K|_T$ on $T$. For the closed immersion $i:Z\hookrightarrow T$, localize at $t$. The map $\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{T,t}\to T$ is affine ind-Zariski, since $T$ is affine and ring localization is the filtered colimit of principal localizations. The new base-change lemma identifies $L|_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{Z,t}}$ with $i_t^!(K|_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{T,t}})$. Composing $i_t$ with the closed point immersion of $\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{Z,t}$ and using Step 1 identifies $C_{\bar w}(L)$ with $C_{\bar t}(K|_T)$. The residue fields of a closed immersion agree, so these comparisons use the same geometric fibres. Hence both $C_{\bar w}(K)\cong C_{\bar w}(L)$ follow.

source.place: Definition 1.4.1: both vertical isomorphisms of the costalk comparison square

proof.text:
By [prop-weil-pbc-universal-homeomorphism-topos], inverse image by $
u$ is an equivalence of small etale topoi. It induces an equivalence on $\Lambda$-module sheaves: inverse image takes the constant coefficient ring to the same constant ring, and transporting its action transports modules and module morphisms. On injective resolutions this exact equivalence computes derived sections and supported sections. Indeed it preserves sections on the terminal object and on the open generic point, and therefore preserves the kernel of restriction to that open, which is the supported-sections functor of [def-pur-etale-derived-supported-sections]. Thus
$$R\Gamma_{\{z_0\}}(Z,L)\cong R\Gamma_{\{\widetilde z_0\}}(\widetilde Z,
u^*L).$$
Since $Z$ is strictly henselian local, Step 2 identifies the left side with its closed geometric costalk. At the generic point of $Z$ the local scheme is $\operatorname{Spec}F$ and its closed point immersion is the identity, so its costalk is just the geometric stalk $L_{ ar\eta}$, unchanged by the identity generic map of $
u$. Combine with Step 7 to obtain both displayed chains in the statement.

source.place: Section 1.3 and the comparison square in Definition 1.4.1: passage to the normalized trait

proof.text: All comparisons come from $\Lambda$-linear operations on complexes, hence commute with shifts. Define twists by roots of unity [def-asd-finite-etale-tate-twist] with $N=\ell$, $A=\mathbf F_\ell$, and define negative twists by dual tensor powers. By [lem-asd-finite-etale-twist-line] the first twist is an etale locally free line. Each supported-cohomology expression in the final comparisons is on a strictly henselian local scheme. Choose a trivializing etale neighbourhood above its closed point. By [lem-sbc-strict-henselian-etale-neighbourhood-section] this neighbourhood has a section, so its basis pulls back to a global basis on that strict local scheme. For the specialization chains choose the basis on $T=X_{(\bar x)}$ and pull it to $Z$, $\widetilde Z$ and the further strict localizations; at a geometric fibre use the induced basis. Tensoring by a twist is now tensoring by a free rank-one constant module throughout the strict-local comparison. All maps are the untwisted maps in these bases, including the supported restriction kernels. A different basis multiplies by a unit and commutes with these linear maps, so the identification is independent of the basis. Finally roots of unity pull back as the representing equation $t^\ell=1$, so the topological equivalence preserves that line and its duals. This gives the claimed twist compatibility.
